accuracy.evidence: Checked against Royal Museums Greenwich guides to the Plough and finding the North Star, the IAU constellation list and NASA Space Place. The Plough is 7 bright stars and an asterism inside the constellation Ursa Major (stated in the adult text); pointers Merak and Dubhe are about 5.4 degrees apart and Polaris about 28.7 degrees from Dubhe, so 'about 5 gaps' (5.3) is right and the lab's tick marks use 5.3 gaps; Polaris is about the 48th brightest star and Sirius the brightest at night; the sky turns about 15 degrees an hour round Polaris, so 6 hours is a quarter turn, anticlockwise when facing north as drawn; the Plough is circumpolar from the UK (Alkaid declination about +49), so it is visible on any clear night; Cassiopeia's W of 5 stars lies on the far side of Polaris. Parameterised answers 7-a, 5-a and 5*a stay positive whole numbers at every corner.

misconceptions.evidence: Targets documented children's astronomy beliefs (Sharp 1996, UK primary children; Comins 2001 'Heavenly Errors'; Vosniadou and Brewer 1994): the North Star is the brightest (pointer predict, bright decoy feedback, robot fact 1, p4, challenge 'bright'), stars go away in the day (robot fact 3, p5, challenge 'day' and 'moon'), the Plough stays still and the North Star moves (turn predict, turn feedback, m4, challenge 'still'), an upside-down Plough is a new pattern (turned-round predict, m5, challenge 'flip'), a mirror-flipped Plough (shape decoy, m8), and using the handle or near-pan stars as pointers (point feedback, p3, challenge 'pointer').

lab_distinct.evidence: flagplough is about finding star patterns and star-hopping: picking the 7 Plough stars out of a field, choosing the pointer pair and following a 5-gap line to Polaris past a brighter decoy, moving the night on in 2-hour steps with faint trails of the Plough turning round Polaris, and choosing the Plough among a mirror image, Cassiopeia's W and a random 7-star zigzag. No other lab works with the night sky this way; flagstar (the Sun is a star) and flagmoonph (Moon phases) are about other mechanisms, and the lab_distinct gate measures it under 30% against every lab.

lab_teaches.evidence: The child discovers each idea by doing: the bright decoy is refused because it is off the pointer line, so brightness is not how the North Star is found; after three '+2 hours' taps the faint old Plough positions show it swinging round while the middle star never moved; the turned-round skies show the same shape in a new direction while the mirror image is refused. Done messages state the rule only after the task.

predictions.evidence: Three predictions with tempting wrong options the lab then disproves: 'Yes, the brightest of all' (a brighter star sits off the line and is refused), 'The Plough stays still' (the Plough visibly swings a quarter turn in 6 hours while the North Star stays put), and 'No, it is a new pattern' (the upside-down and sideways Ploughs are accepted as the Plough).

challenge_feedback.evidence: Six challenge questions with every wrong option tagged and answered with its own message: w (5 stars is Cassiopeia's W), count (3 is only the handle), pointer, bright, planet, day, moon (the Moon is too small to hide the stars), still, flip and apart. In the lab, wrong taps also name the slip: handle star or handle-side pan star as a pointer, the brighter off-line star, a Plough star as the still star, a mirror-flipped Plough.

readability.evidence: Kid paragraphs use short sentences with one idea each (what a constellation is, finding the pointers, the North Star is not brightest but stays still, stars are there by day); validate_lessons readability passes for kid and adult text. Lab banners stay short, e.g. 'Tap the 2 pointer stars (0 of 2)' and 'Sky 1 of 3: which one is the Plough?'. Star names Merak and Dubhe appear only as button labels next to the word pointer.

no_filler.evidence: Every kid sentence is a fact, a step or a warning; adult paragraphs give the standard and key words (with the Big Dipper and Ursa Major names), the brightest-star mistake with the real ranking, the other mix-ups and what each lab scene does. The content gate finds no filler phrases and the explanation is under 12% similar to any other lesson.

mobile.evidence: Checked 360 px phone screenshots in light and dark for every scene before and after Show me: Plough stars are 5 px dots with 24 px tap radius and at least about 30 px apart, the pointer scene fits the Plough, the 5-gap line and the North Star in one view, the turn scene keeps the whole quarter turn on screen with the +2 hours tile top left away from the Plough's path, and the three skies sit side by side with stars at 4.5 px. Every scene has large labelled buttons under the canvas (56 px young-lab buttons).

accessibility.evidence: Every canvas action has a labelled button twin: Next handle star or Next pan star and A star off the pattern; Merak, Dubhe and Megrez buttons, then Star on the line and The brightest star; +2 hours, The middle star and A Plough star; Left, Middle and Right sky; Right and Slip. The canvas aria-label is updated with every message, challenge feedback is a polite live region, the walk gate's axe run is clean in both themes on desktop and iPhone 13, and a 360 px check found no lesson control under 44 x 44 px.
